title: A Generalized Unified Character Code: Western European and CJK Sections
summary: An April 1st joke RFC describing a fully unified coded character set for Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, and CJK-based scripts. It is not a complete specification. It is informational and humorous.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st joke invents a complicated character code for several writing systems. Its unusual rules and examples make the proposal satirical.

questions: how does this character code work
what is the unified character code in rfc 5242
subtitle: An April 1st joke proposing one elaborate character code for several scripts.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke claims that internationalized domain names need a new unified character code for Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, and CJK scripts.
tldr.mechanism: It proposes base characters, combining marks, modifiers, and positioning controls, with a canonical form and 23-bit values.
tldr.outcome: The IESG note says this is not an IETF document and not a candidate for an Internet Standard.

today: RFC 5242 is an Informational April 1st joke document. Its IESG note says it is not an IETF document or candidate for an Internet Standard.

sections.title: A Unified Character-Code Proposal
sections.content:
The memo proposes a unified coded character set for scripts based on Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, and Chinese characters. It says the design borrows terminology from Unicode but takes a radically different approach.

The stated principles include treating alike-looking glyphs alike, preferring combining characters, and choosing sans-serif forms. The RFC's publication note says it is not an IETF document.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal tries to combine several scripts in one system. Its principles lead to deliberately odd character constructions.

sections.title: Characters Built from Components
sections.content:
The design defines base characters, nonspacing marks, case indicators, joining indicators, positioning indicators, and repetition indicators. Uppercase letters use a UC modifier after a lowercase base character.

Some letters are assembled from other symbols and modifiers. The RFC's example says “w” is built from two “u” characters joined by ZWCJ, rather than being a base character.
sections.plainLanguage: Letters can be assembled from smaller shapes and modifiers. The RFC's joke example constructs w from two joined u characters.

sections.title: Code Values, Canonical Form, and Security
sections.content:
The memo assigns 23 bits to each character value and divides value ranges among controls, marks, reserved space, and characters. It requires a canonical representation: use the shorter sequence, and use the sequence with the smaller sum of octet values when lengths tie.

It asks IANA to maintain a character registry and claims the system would reduce some visual-confusion attacks. The security section also acknowledges that visual confusion would not be completely eliminated.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC assigns values to character pieces and chooses one allowed spelling for each character. Its security claims are also qualified by examples of remaining visual confusion.
